'''South Norwalk''' is a neighborhood in [[Norwalk, Connecticut]] which corresponds to the city's Second Taxing District.<ref>{{cite web |title=Taxing District Elections |url=http://www.norwalkct.org/1104/Taxing-District-Elections |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220308081837/https://www.norwalkct.org/1104/Taxing-District-Elections |archive-date=2022-03-08 |access-date=2022-07-05 |website=City of Norwalk |publisher=CivicPlus |df=mdy-all}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Schuetz |first=R. A. |date=2017-10-07 |title=Municipal mashup: Mergers long ago created Norwalk's taxing system |url=https://www.thehour.com/news/article/Municipal-mashup-Mergers-long-ago-created-12260541.php |access-date=2022-07-05 |website=The Hour |language=en-US}}</ref> Often referred to as '''SoNo''',<ref>{{Cite web |title=Visit SoNo |url=http://www.visitsono.com/ |access-date=2022-07-05 |website=www.visitsono.com}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Chumney |first=Richard |date=2021-06-24 |title=Zoning board approves 150-unit apartment building in South Norwalk |url=https://www.thehour.com/news/article/Zoning-board-approves-150-unit-apartment-building-16272270.php |access-date=2022-07-05 |website=The Hour |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Craven |first=John |date=2022-05-16 |title=South Norwalk train station to undergo $6M redevelopment plan |url=https://longisland.news12.com/south-norwalk-train-station-to-undergo-6m-redevelopment-plan |access-date=2022-07-05 |website=News 12 - Long Island}}</ref> the neighborhood was originally settled as Old Well, then chartered as the city of South Norwalk on August 18, 1870. The cities of Norwalk and South Norwalk were incorporated on June 6, 1913. South Norwalk underwent major redevelopment during the early 21st century, with many new apartments being constructed,<ref name=":1" /> often in close proximity to [[South Norwalk station]],<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> and generally more expensive than existing housing.<ref name=":2" />

South Norwalk is a diverse neighborhood both from a socioeconomic and racial perspective.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}

The neighborhood hosts the annual SoNo Arts Festival, an event that showcases local artists, businesses, and musical acts.<ref>{{Cite web |title=SoNo ARTS FESTIVAL |url=https://www.gordonfinearts.org/xxx |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220705142427/https://www.gordonfinearts.org/xxx |archive-date=2022-07-05 |access-date=2022-07-05 |website=GORDON FINE ARTS |language=en-US}}</ref> The annual [[Norwalk Oyster Festival]], sponsored by the Norwalk Seaport Association, is held at Veteran's Memorial Park, across the [[Norwalk Harbor]] in [[East Norwalk]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Norwalk Oyster Festival 2022 |url=https://www.seaport.org/norwalk-oyster-festival |access-date=2022-07-05 |website=www.seaport.org |language=en}}</ref>

==History==
[[File:South Norwalk and Norwalk, Conn. (2674626278).jpg|thumb|Map of South Norwalk and Norwalk, CT]]

===Old Well===
The area of present-day South Norwalk developed out of a local [[well]] referred to as the "Old Well", where sailing ships would refill their water [[casks]].<ref name=":3" /> Said well was in service since at least 1738, when a deed referred to nearby Washington Street as "the highway that leads to ye landing place called Ye Old Well".<ref name=":3" /> The well's location was depicted as east of Water Street, and about 75 feet South of Washington Street in a 1867 map by American [[Cartography|cartographer]] Frederick W. Beers<!--Q27056880-->,<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{cite web |date=1867 |title=Plan of Norwalk, Plan of South Norwalk. Fairfield County, Connecticut |url=http://www.davidrumsey.com/luna/servlet/s/yx48f4 |website=[[David Rumsey Historical Map Collection]] |publisher=Beers, Ellis, & Soule}}</ref> although the exact location is unknown, though presumed to be near the site of Donovan's Tavern, since sailors are said to have frequented the tavern.<ref name=":3" />

The area evolved into a settlement named Old Well. after the well, and was involved in coastal trade, manufacturing, and shipbuilding, as well as having many farms with diversified crops.<ref name=":3">{{cite web |last=Booth |first=Dick |title=HISTORIC SOUTH NORWALK |url=http://www.norwalkct.org/DocumentCenter/View/686/HistoricSoNwlk |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220705143914/https://www.norwalkct.org/DocumentCenter/View/686/HistoricSoNwlk |archive-date=2022-07-05 |access-date=2022-07-05 |website=norwalkct.org}}</ref>

“Old Well was scarcely a village in those days, but rather a group of farms, and the well which gave the place its name was on Water Street, near the corner of Haviland street, on the property of Eliakim Raymond, a patriarch of several Norwalk lines.  His house stood at the corner of Washington and Water streets before the Revolution and was burned with rest of the town."<ref name="auto">{{cite web|url=https://archive.org/details/norwalkaftertwoh00weed|title=Norwalk after two hundred & fifty years, an account of the celebration of the 250th anniversary of the charter of the town, 1651--September 11th--1901; including historical sketches of churches, schools, old homes, institutions, eminent men, patriotic and benevolent work, together with the record of soldiers and sailors enlisted in Norwalk from 1676 to 1898. The civic progress in the last century and statistics of commerce and other miscellany of local interest|first1=Samuel Richards|last1=Weed|last2=Norwalk Historical and Memorial Library Association|date=August 2, 2018|publisher=South Norwalk, Conn., C. A. Freeman|access-date=August 2, 2018|via=Internet Archive|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170525012532/https://archive.org/details/norwalkaftertwoh00weed|archive-date=May 25, 2017|url-status=live|df=mdy-all}}</ref>

===City of South Norwalk===
"[[Norwalk, Connecticut|Norwalk]] was made a borough in 1836, and the village of Old Well, named from an ancient well where vessels were supplied with water, was incorporated into a city in 1868, and named South Norwalk two years afterward."<ref>{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/ahistorynewengl00unkngoog|page=[https://archive.org/details/ahistorynewengl00unkngoog/page/n334 300]|quote=South Norwalk Original Settlement.|title=A History of New England: Containing Historical and Descriptive Sketches of the Counties, Cities and Principal Towns of the Six New England States, Including, in Its List of Contributors, More Than Sixty Literary Men and Women, Representing Every County in New England|first1=R. H.|last1=Howard|first2=Henry E.|last2=Crocker|date=August 2, 1879|publisher=Crocker & Company|access-date=August 2, 2018|via=Internet Archive|df=mdy-all}}</ref> "South Norwalk, formerly called "Old Well" was organized a city August 18, 1870, under a charter granted by the [[Connecticut General Assembly|Legislature of Connecticut]], July 5 of the same year".<ref name="auto" /> In 1873, the City of South Norwalk was incorporated within the Town of Norwalk, although it maintained its city status and retained control over its own assets.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4">{{cite web |last=Bullen |first=Isabel |date=June 14, 2014 |title=The History of the Second Taxing District |url=http://discovernorwalk.com/historic-sono/the-second-taxing-district/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170804052244/http://discovernorwalk.com/historic-sono/the-second-taxing-district/ |archive-date=August 4, 2017 |access-date=August 2, 2018 |website=Discovernorwalk.com |df=mdy-all}}</ref> "The 1870 charter was revised by the Legislature April 19, 1882, and the city continued its existence under this revised charter until May 27, 1897, when the Legislature approved a revised and amended charter, under which the city has since continued and worked."<ref name="auto"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FFhDAAAAYAAJ&q=City+of+South+Norwalk+Charter|title=Charter of the City, Pub ... 1898|first=South Norwalk (Norwalk)|last=Conn.)|date=August 2, 1898|publisher=City Printing Company|access-date=August 2, 2018|via=Google Books|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160617061406/https://books.google.com/books?id=FFhDAAAAYAAJ&printsec=frontcover&dq=City+of+South+Norwalk+Charter&hl=en&sa=X&ved=0CDEQ6AEwAGoVChMImd7gn9StxwIVxD4-Ch2TiQTK|archive-date=June 17, 2016|url-status=live|df=mdy-all}}</ref>

Around this time, Norwalk had refused to share its [[water system]] with South Norwalk, contributing to a sense of ill will between the two cities, which would compete for economic development throughout subsequent decades.<ref name=":0" />

"In the 1800s, [[Industrialisation|industrialization]] started to take place--large factories manufacturing goods such as firearms, buttons, shoes, cloth and hats were increasing in Connecticut and in Norwalk.  Workers came up from [[Chesapeake Bay|Chesapeake]], [[Maryland]], to work as oystermen. Wealthy owners and managers of businesses lived on ''Golden Hill'' overlooking South Norwalk. Immigrants came into Norwalk from many places. One of the largest [group] to come here in the early 1900s was the [[Hungarians]]; there were also many Eastern European [[Jews]] and [[Italians]], among others."<ref>{{cite book|last1=Grant|first1=Lisa Wilson|title=Norwalk|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=f_-aAwAAQBAJ&q=Hungarian+population+South+Norwalk&pg=PA8|publisher=Arcadia Publishing|access-date=1 February 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160428054124/https://books.google.com/books?id=f_-aAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA8&lpg=PA8&dq=Hungarian+population+South+Norwalk&source=bl&ots=kcQqEDi2Gt&sig=fcseRhc_mZrYC0RWdiMhZ4JcErw&hl=en&sa=X&ved=0CFwQ6AEwDGoVChMI5-qz4uSSyQIVhWImCh1F5wzE#v=onepage&q=Hungarian%20population%20South%20Norwalk&f=false|archive-date=April 28, 2016|url-status=live|df=mdy-all|isbn=9781467121163|year=2014}}</ref>

[[Trolley (horse-drawn)|Horse-drawn trolleys]] began serving South Norwalk in the 1860s, until being upgraded to [[Tram|electric trolleys]] in 1894.<ref name=":3" />

Industrialization in South Norwalk resulted in the city becoming a center for local industry, hosting [[South Norwalk station|its own railroad station]], the [[Norwalk Harbor]], an electric trolley system, its own water company, electric company, and well-developed school system.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" />

==== Consolidation into Norwalk ====
Despite the industrialization of South Norwalk, various economic forces pressured the city South Norwalk to merge into Norwalk, as both cities were often too small independent of one another to host large industries.<ref name=":0" /> South Norwalk was hesitant to consolidate into Norwalk, due to South Norwalk's industry surpassing that of Norwalk.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" /> South Norwalk, alongside [[East Norwalk]], even tried to leave the Town of Norwalk altogether in 1902, with South Norwalk's mayor Mortimer M. Lee touting that South Norwalk had "a large water system, a splendid electric light plant, a separate sewer system, a public library and a library building and schools second to none".<ref name=":4" /> In 1903 the Connecticut State Legislature passed a bill to create an independent Town of South Norwalk, but it was vetoed by then-governor [[Abiram Chamberlain]].<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Meriden Morning Record - Google News Archive Search |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2513&dat=19030409&id=53VHAAAAIBAJ&pg=1158,3910625&hl=en |access-date=August 2, 2018 |website=news.google.com}}</ref>

As a compromise, Norwalk allowed for South Norwalk, East Norwalk, and [[Rowayton, Connecticut|Rowayton]] to join Norwalk as taxing districts, allowing them to largely maintain their own municipal services while within Norwalk.<ref name=":0" />

=== Within Norwalk ===
[[File:SoNo Historic Washington Street 1.jpg|thumb|A street scene along a portion of Washington Street, part of the [[South Main and Washington Streets Historic District]] created in 1977]]
{{further|History of Norwalk, Connecticut}}In 1935, South Norwalk's trolley system was discontinued, and replaced by a bus service.<ref name=":3" />

South Norwalk began suffering from a period of [[deindustrialization]] in the 1950s, as many industries, including Norwalk's sizable [[hat]] industry, either went into decline or relocated out of [[New England]].<ref name=":4" /> This industrial decay led to the enactment of various [[urban renewal]] projects beginning in the 1960s, namely, the demolition of older buildings and factories along western Washington Street to build new offices, a shopping center, and low-cost housing.<ref name=":4" /> The Norwalk Redevelopment Agency planned to continue this effort in the 1970s, with plans to replace the older buildings along eastern Washington Street, but were thwarted by local residents, who successfully got the buildings added to the [[National Register of Historic Places]] in 1977.<ref name=":4" />

In 1988, the [[Maritime Aquarium at Norwalk|Maritime Aquarium]] was opened in a disused factory building.<ref name=":4" />

During the 21st century, South Norwalk has seen a period of redevelopment centered around the construction of new apartments, many of which are located near South Norwalk Station.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />

== Geography ==
Administratively, the Norwalk Second Taxing District, synonymous with South Norwalk, is bordered by [[U.S. Route 1|Route 1]] (locally signed as Connecticut Avenue) to the north, and the [[Norwalk Harbor]] and the [[Norwalk River]] to the east.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=Archived copy |url=http://www.norwalkct.org/DocumentCenter/View/4745 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150115001535/http://www.norwalkct.org/DocumentCenter/View/4745 |archive-date=January 15, 2015 |access-date=March 27, 2017 |df=mdy-all}}</ref> The neighborhood's southern border runs from Windsor Place to Neptune Avenue, up against the Norwalk River, and the neighborhood's western border runs from Windsor Place up to Connecticut Avenue.<ref name=":5" />

== Demographics ==
All of South Norwalk is represented by the 06854 [[ZIP Code]], which also includes some areas to its south and west.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=ZCTA5 06854 |url=https://data.census.gov/cedsci/profile?g=860XX00US06854 |access-date=2022-07-05 |website=data.census.gov |publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]]}}</ref> As of 2020, the ZIP Code has an average family income of $74,597, slightly below the Connecticut average of $79,855; the [[poverty]] rate is 14.5%, higher than the Connecticut total of 9.8%; 34.2% of the population has a [[Bachelor's degree]] or higher, below the state total of 40.0%; the ZIP code has an employment rate 65.4%, higher than the Connecticut total of 61.7%; 22.0% of the population lacks health care coverage, significantly higher than the state total of 5.1%; 22.5% of the population is under 18 years old, slightly higher than the state total of 20.6%; the average household size is 3.25, slightly higher than the state total of 3.08.<ref name=":6" />

==The SoNo Collection==
{{Main|The SoNo Collection}}
The SoNo Collection is a 700,000 square foot mall located next to Interstate 95 and Route 7 that was opened in October 2019. It was built by [[Brookfield Properties]] and is the fourth mall in the [[Fairfield County, Connecticut|Fairfield County]]. It features southern Connecticut's only locations of the department stores [[Nordstrom]] and [[Bloomingdale's]].<ref>{{cite web |title=The Sono Collection |url=https://ggpnorwalk.com/}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Lurye |first1=Rebecca |title=SoNo Collection, Norwalk's New Mall, A Retail Anomaly |url=http://www.courant.com/business/hc-biz-norwalk-new-mall-20171116-story.html |website=courant.com |access-date=2 August 2018}}</ref>

[[File:NorwalkCTNorwalkMuseum80122007.JPG|thumb|Former City Hall]]
* [[Norwalk City Hall]]<ref name="nationalregisterofhistoricplaces.com">{{cite web|url=http://www.nationalregisterofhistoricplaces.com/ct/fairfield/state4.html|title=National Register of Historical Places - CONNECTICUT (CT), Fairfield County|website=Nationalregisterofhistoricplaces.com|access-date=August 2, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170301181729/http://www.nationalregisterofhistoricplaces.com/ct/fairfield/state4.html|archive-date=March 1, 2017|url-status=live|df=mdy-all}}</ref> Completed in 1912, when South Norwalk was an autonomous municipal entity, 41 North Main Street originally served as the South Norwalk Town Hall.

The Norwalk Historical Society along with the Norwalk Historical Commission reopened the Norwalk Historical Society Museum at the Lockwood House at 141 East Avenue.  The archives, genealogy and unframed photographs was placed with the  “History Room”  at the Norwalk Public Library Main branch (1 Belden Avenue, Norwalk, CT). It includes items from the four collections: City of Norwalk, Lockwood family, Norwalk Historical Society and the Connecticut Daughters of the American Revolution (DAR) and Norwalk-Village Green Chapter.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://norwalkhistoricalsociety.org/about/visit-us/|title=Visit Us|website=Norwalkhistoricalsociety.org|access-date=February 11, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170427191005/http://norwalkhistoricalsociety.org/about/visit-us/|archive-date=April 27, 2017|url-status=live|df=mdy-all}}</ref>

* [[South Main and Washington Streets Historic District]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationalregisterofhistoricplaces.com/ct/fairfield/districts.html|title=National Register of Historical Places - CONNECTICUT (CT), Fairfield County|website=Nationalregisterofhistoricplaces.com|access-date=August 2, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170817123716/http://www.nationalregisterofhistoricplaces.com/ct/fairfield/districts.html|archive-date=August 17, 2017|url-status=live|df=mdy-all}}</ref> The district encompasses 35 buildings and two other structures (including the [[South Norwalk Railroad Bridge]]).

==Emergency services==
The Norwalk Police Department<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.norwalkct.org/index.aspx?nid=139|title=Police Department - Norwalk, CT - Official Website|website=Norwalkct.org|access-date=August 2, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170108091553/http://norwalkct.org/index.aspx?nid=139|archive-date=January 8, 2017|url-status=live|df=mdy-all}}</ref> is located at 1 Monroe Street near the heart of SoNo. The Norwalk Fire Department currently operates two Fire Stations in or near South Norwalk:<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.norwalkct.org/index.aspx?NID=399|title=Stations / Station Map - Norwalk, CT - Official Website|website=Norwalkct.org|access-date=August 2, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161224095942/http://norwalkct.org/index.aspx?nid=399|archive-date=December 24, 2016|url-status=live|df=mdy-all}}</ref>
